lessons.title: Frontend observability: real user monitoring, web vitals, errors and replay
lessons.summary: Field vs lab data, collecting Core Web Vitals with the web-vitals library, making production JavaScript errors debuggable, and the privacy and cost trade-offs of session replay.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Your backend dashboards can be green while users suffer: a 3 MB JavaScript bundle on a mid-range Android phone, a third-party script blocking the main thread, a CDN edge misbehaving in one country, a React error that blanks the page only in Safari. **Real User Monitoring (RUM)** measures what actually happens in users' browsers: load and interaction performance, JavaScript errors, failed requests, and sometimes a replay of the session.

RUM is **field data**. Lighthouse and WebPageTest give **lab data**: one controlled device and network, reproducible, great for debugging and CI budgets, but not your users. Google's Chrome UX Report (CrUX) is field data for public sites, aggregated over 28 days. You want both: lab to catch regressions before release, field to know the truth.

## What to collect

```text
browser                                   collector / vendor                 analysis
-------                                   ------------------                 --------
web-vitals (LCP, INP, CLS, FCP, TTFB) --\
JS errors + stack + release           ---+--> sendBeacon / fetch keepalive --> ingest endpoint --> p75 by page, device,
fetch/XHR failures + timing           ---|    (batched, sampled)              (sampling, PII      country, release
navigation + resource timing          ---|                                     scrub, source      error grouping
user/session ids, route, release      --/                                      maps applied)      replay on error
optional: session replay (DOM diffs)
```

### Core Web Vitals
Google's user-centric metrics, judged at the **75th percentile** of page loads, split by mobile and desktop:

| Metric | Measures | Good | Poor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LCP** Largest Contentful Paint | When the main content (largest image or text block) rendered | <= 2.5 s | > 4 s |
| **INP** Interaction to Next Paint | Responsiveness: latency from input to the next frame, roughly the worst interaction of the visit | <= 200 ms | > 500 ms |
| **CLS** Cumulative Layout Shift | Visual stability: unexpected layout movement (largest burst of shifts) | <= 0.1 | > 0.25 |

INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. FID only measured the input delay of the first interaction; INP covers all interactions including processing and rendering time. Supporting metrics: **TTFB** (server and network), **FCP** (first paint of anything).

### Errors
- Uncaught exceptions (`window.onerror` / `error` event), unhandled promise rejections (`unhandledrejection`), React error boundaries, console errors if you choose.
- Failed network calls (status, duration, endpoint template), including CORS failures that surface as opaque `TypeError: Failed to fetch`.
- Resource load failures (a chunk that 404s after a deploy: the classic `ChunkLoadError` when users hold an old HTML page that references deleted hashed bundles).

## Measuring web vitals yourself
The `web-vitals` library from the Chrome team handles the edge cases (back/forward cache restores, background tabs, reporting the final CLS value when the page is hidden):

```ts
import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS, onTTFB, type Metric } from "web-vitals/attribution";

const queue: object[] = [];

function report(metric: Metric) {
  queue.push({
    name: metric.name,                // "LCP" | "INP" | "CLS" | "TTFB"
    value: Math.round(metric.name === "CLS" ? metric.value * 1000 : metric.value),
    rating: metric.rating,            // "good" | "needs-improvement" | "poor"
    id: metric.id,                    // unique per page load, for dedupe
    navigationType: metric.navigationType,
    route: getRouteTemplate(),        // your router's pattern, "/product/[slug]", not the full URL
    release: import.meta.env.VITE_RELEASE,
    // attribution build tells you WHY: LCP element, slow interaction target, shifted node
    debug: metric.name === "INP" ? metric.attribution.interactionTarget
         : metric.name === "LCP" ? metric.attribution.target
         : undefined,
  });
}

function flush() {
  if (!queue.length) return;
  navigator.sendBeacon("/rum", JSON.stringify(queue.splice(0)));
}

onLCP(report); onINP(report); onCLS(report); onTTFB(report);
addEventListener("visibilitychange", () => { if (document.visibilityState === "hidden") flush(); });
```

Notes:
- **Send on `visibilitychange` to hidden**, not `unload` or `beforeunload`: those do not fire reliably on mobile and `unload` breaks the back/forward cache. `navigator.sendBeacon` (or `fetch` with `keepalive: true`) survives the page going away.
- **Report route templates**, not full URLs, so you can aggregate by page type and avoid leaking ids and tokens from query strings.
- Next.js exposes `useReportWebVitals` for the same purpose.
- The **attribution** build reports the LCP element and its resource load phases, the element and event behind a slow INP, and the nodes that shifted, which turns "INP is bad" into "the filter dropdown handler takes 400 ms".

## Error tracking
Tools like Sentry, Bugsnag, Rollbar, Datadog RUM or open-source options (GlitchTip, Highlight's OSS edition) group errors by fingerprint, show counts, affected users, browsers and releases.

Make it useful:
- **Upload source maps** at build time (privately, to the error tracker, not public on your CDN) so minified stacks become real file and line numbers.
- **Tag the release** (git sha) so you can say "this error started in release a3f9c1" and correlate with deploys.
- **Cross-origin scripts** report only `Script error.` with no details unless served with CORS headers and loaded with the `crossorigin` attribute.
- **Filter noise**: browser extensions, ad blockers, bots and ancient browsers create errors you cannot fix. Use allowlists of your own script origins.
- **Breadcrumbs**: the last N clicks, navigations and network calls before the error are often more useful than the stack.
- **Connect to the backend**: propagate `traceparent` on `fetch` calls (OTel web SDK or the vendor SDK) so a slow API call in the browser links to its backend trace. This requires the API to allow the header via CORS.

## Session replay: value and trade-offs
Session replay records DOM snapshots and mutations (not video) plus input events, then reconstructs the session in a player. rrweb is the open-source library many products build on.

**Value:** you watch exactly what the user did before an error or rage click. It resolves "cannot reproduce" bugs in minutes.

**Costs and risks:**
- **Privacy.** Replays can capture everything on screen: names, addresses, messages, health or financial data. Mask all text and inputs by default (most SDKs offer `maskAllText` / `blockAllMedia`), unmask only reviewed safe areas, never record password, payment or sensitive screens, disclose it in the privacy policy, and check consent requirements (GDPR, CCPA).
- **Performance.** Serialising the DOM and observing mutations costs main-thread time and bandwidth; on heavy pages it can hurt the very INP you are measuring.
- **Volume and money.** Recording every session is expensive. Typical setups sample a small fraction of sessions (Sentry's `replaysSessionSampleRate`) and keep a buffer that is only uploaded when an error occurs (`replaysOnErrorSampleRate`).

## Sampling and data quality
- Vitals are small; you can often keep 100% or sample 10-50% on high-traffic sites. Replays and full resource timing deserve much lower rates.
- **Segment** before judging: p75 for all users can look fine while p75 on low-end Android in India is poor. Break down by device class, connection type (`navigator.connection` where supported), country, route and release.
- **Ad blockers** block many vendor RUM endpoints; serving the collector from your own domain (first-party proxy) improves coverage.
- **Bots** skew data; filter by user agent and behaviour.

## Trade-offs and when not to use RUM
- Small internal tools rarely need full RUM; error tracking with source maps is the 80/20.
- Third-party RUM scripts are themselves JavaScript on your critical path; load them asynchronously and measure their cost.
- Field data is noisy and lagging (you see a regression only after users hit it). Pair with lab budgets in CI (Lighthouse CI) and canary releases.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- Measuring averages instead of p75 and distributions.
- Using `unload` to send data; losing most mobile beacons.
- Shipping public source maps unintentionally, exposing source code.
- Full URLs with tokens or emails in RUM payloads.
- Treating a "Script error." flood as actionable instead of fixing CORS on your CDN.
- Ignoring `ChunkLoadError` after deploys; fix with keeping old assets for a while, or reloading on chunk failure.
- Only looking at Lighthouse scores, which run on one fast simulated device, and calling performance "done".

## In the interview
**What they probe:** for frontend and full-stack roles, whether you know the Core Web Vitals with thresholds, lab vs field, how to collect metrics reliably, how to make production errors debuggable, and the privacy judgement around session replay.

**60-second answer outline:**
1. Backend metrics miss the user's device, network and JavaScript; RUM measures the real experience.
2. Collect LCP, INP, CLS (p75 thresholds 2.5 s, 200 ms, 0.1) plus TTFB with the web-vitals library, sent via sendBeacon on visibilitychange, tagged with route template and release.
3. Error tracking with private source maps, release tags, breadcrumbs, noise filtering, and trace propagation to the backend.
4. Session replay sampled and on-error, with masking by default and consent.
5. Segment by device, country and release; pair with lab budgets in CI.

**Follow-ups to expect:** Why did INP replace FID? How do you find which interaction causes a poor INP? Why is your RUM data missing 30% of mobile sessions? How do you make minified stack traces readable without publishing source?
keyPoints: RUM measures real devices and networks; lab tools like Lighthouse are reproducible but are not your users.
Core Web Vitals are judged at p75: LCP <= 2.5 s, INP <= 200 ms, CLS <= 0.1. INP replaced FID in March 2024.
Send beacons on visibilitychange to hidden with sendBeacon, tagged with route template and release, never full URLs.
Upload source maps privately, tag releases and propagate traceparent on fetch so browser errors link to backend traces.
Session replay needs masking by default, consent, and sampling (often only on error) because of privacy, performance and cost.
interview: How would you monitor frontend performance and errors in production?
What are the Core Web Vitals and what are their thresholds?
What are the trade-offs of using session replay?

check.q: Why should RUM beacons be sent on visibilitychange (hidden) rather than on unload?
options: unload fires twice per page
sendBeacon only works inside visibilitychange handlers
unload is unreliable on mobile and blocks the back/forward cache, while visibilitychange fires reliably when the user leaves
visibilitychange compresses the payload automatically
check.why: Mobile browsers often kill pages without firing unload, and unload listeners disable bfcache. visibilitychange to hidden is the last reliable moment.

check.q: What is the 'good' threshold for Interaction to Next Paint at the 75th percentile?
options: 200 ms or less
100 ms or less
500 ms or less
2.5 s or less
check.why: INP is good at <= 200 ms and poor above 500 ms. 2.5 s is the LCP threshold; 100 ms was FID's.

check.q: Your error tracker shows thousands of 'Script error.' events with no stack. What is the likely cause?
options: Source maps were uploaded twice
The scripts are served from another origin without CORS headers and the crossorigin attribute, so the browser hides details
The browser is out of memory
Errors are being sampled at 100%
check.why: Browsers sanitise errors from cross-origin scripts unless the script is loaded with crossorigin and served with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

lessons.title: Profiling: CPU, memory, flame graphs and finding leaks
lessons.summary: Sampling profilers, reading flame graphs correctly, CPU profiling in Node.js and Go, the three-snapshot method for memory leaks, and continuous profiling in production.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Metrics tell you a service got slower or uses more memory. Traces tell you *which span* got slower. A **profiler** tells you *which lines of code* are spending the CPU or holding the memory. It is the last step from symptom to cause, and in interviews it separates people who guess at performance from people who measure.

Profiling comes in a few flavours:
- **CPU (on-CPU) profiling:** where is the CPU time going?
- **Off-CPU / wall-clock profiling:** where are threads *waiting* (locks, I/O, sleep)? A request can be slow while using almost no CPU.
- **Memory / heap profiling:** what is allocated, by whom, and what is still retained (leaks)?
- **Continuous profiling:** low-overhead profiling running in production all the time, stored and queryable like metrics.

## How sampling profilers work

```text
every ~10 ms (e.g. 99 Hz), interrupt each thread and record its call stack:

  t0: main > handleRequest > renderTemplate > escapeHtml
  t1: main > handleRequest > db.query > parseRows
  t2: main > handleRequest > renderTemplate > escapeHtml
  t3: main > handleRequest > renderTemplate > escapeHtml
  ...
aggregate identical stacks -> counts -> "escapeHtml was on CPU in 60% of samples"
```

Sampling keeps overhead low (often around 1-5% at typical rates) and is statistically accurate for hot code; it can miss very short, rare functions. **Instrumenting** profilers that hook every function call are exact but slow and distort timing, so they are rarely used in production. Brendan Gregg samples at 99 Hz rather than 100 to avoid sampling in lockstep with periodic activity.

## Reading a flame graph
Brendan Gregg invented flame graphs to visualise sampled stacks:

```text
          [escapeHtml           ]
     [renderTemplate              ][parseRows]
[handleRequest                                  ][gc]
[main                                                ]
 <------------------- width = share of samples ------------------->
```

- **Y-axis:** stack depth; each box's parent is the box beneath it. (An **icicle graph** is the same thing drawn upside down.)
- **X-axis:** NOT time. Stacks are sorted alphabetically to merge identical frames; **width is proportional to the number of samples** containing that frame.
- **Look for wide plateaus at the top:** a wide box with nothing above it is a function spending CPU in its own code ("self time"). A wide box with many narrow children is spending its time in callees.
- **Flame charts** (Chrome DevTools Performance panel) look similar but the x-axis *is* time, which shows sequence and long tasks rather than aggregate hot spots.
- **Differential flame graphs** compare two profiles (before/after a deploy), colouring frames that grew or shrank.

Common findings: JSON serialisation of huge objects, regex backtracking, logging in hot paths, inefficient ORM hydration, crypto (bcrypt with a high cost on the request path), GC pressure from allocating short-lived objects, and synchronous filesystem calls.

## CPU profiling in practice

### Node.js
```bash
# write a .cpuprofile on exit; open it in Chrome DevTools (Performance or JavaScript Profiler) or speedscope
node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir=./profiles server.js

# attach DevTools to a running process: chrome://inspect
node --inspect=127.0.0.1:9229 server.js
```

Because Node.js runs JavaScript on one thread, a CPU-bound function blocks every other request. Pair CPU profiles with the **event loop delay** metric (`perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()`, also exported by `prom-client`'s default metrics). High event-loop lag with high CPU means hot synchronous code; high latency with low CPU means waiting (I/O, pool exhaustion, downstream), which a CPU profile will not show.

### Go
```go
import _ "net/http/pprof" // registers /debug/pprof/* on the default mux (keep it on an internal port)
```
```bash
go tool pprof -http=:8081 "http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30"   # CPU
go tool pprof -http=:8081 http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap                    # memory
```

### Other runtimes
- **Python:** `py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid <pid>` samples a running process without code changes.
- **JVM:** async-profiler, Java Flight Recorder.
- **Any native process on Linux:** `perf record -F 99 -g -p <pid>`, then Gregg's FlameGraph scripts.

## Memory profiling and finding leaks
In garbage-collected runtimes a "leak" means objects that are still **reachable** but no longer needed. The GC cannot free them because something references them.

Symptoms: memory grows steadily across hours (a sawtooth whose troughs keep rising), GC time increases, latency gets worse, and eventually the container is OOM-killed (Kubernetes reports `OOMKilled`, exit code 137) and restarts, which hides the leak behind a periodic recovery.

```text
heap used
  ^           /|        /|        /|
  |       /| / |    /| / |    /| / |      troughs rising = leak
  |   /| / |/  |/| / |/  |/| / |/  |
  |  / |/      |/        |/        |  <- OOMKilled, restart
  +-------------------------------------> time
```

**The three-snapshot technique** (Node.js or browser):
1. Warm up the service, take heap snapshot A.
2. Run the suspected operation many times (e.g. 10,000 requests), force or wait for GC, take snapshot B.
3. Repeat the load, take snapshot C.
4. In DevTools Memory panel, compare: objects allocated between A and B that *still exist in C* are leak candidates. Sort by retained size, then read the **retainers** chain to find what holds them (a module-level `Map`, an event emitter, a closure).

```ts
import { writeHeapSnapshot } from "node:v8";
// expose on an internal admin route or signal; snapshots pause the process and can be large
process.on("SIGUSR2", () => console.log("heap snapshot:", writeHeapSnapshot()));
// or start node with --heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2
```

Typical leak causes:
- **Unbounded caches**: `const cache = new Map()` keyed by user or request id, never evicted. Use an LRU with a max size or TTL.
- **Event listeners** added per request and never removed (Node warns with `MaxListenersExceededWarning` after 10 on one emitter).
- **Closures** capturing large objects in long-lived callbacks or timers (`setInterval` never cleared).
- **Global arrays** used as debug buffers.
- **Promises that never settle**, holding their whole context.
- In browsers: **detached DOM nodes** still referenced from JavaScript, listeners on `window` from unmounted components, subscriptions without cleanup in `useEffect`.

Allocation profiling (`--heap-prof`, Go's `alloc_space`) answers a different question: who allocates the most (GC pressure), even if it is freed quickly.

## Continuous profiling
Instead of attaching a profiler during an incident (when it is often too late), run a low-overhead sampler on every instance all the time and store the profiles, labelled by service, version, region and pod.

- Open source: **Grafana Pyroscope**, **Parca** (eBPF-based, profiles any process on the node without code changes).
- Vendors: Datadog Continuous Profiler, Google Cloud Profiler, Polar Signals, and others.
- **OpenTelemetry** is adding profiles as a signal, so profiles can be correlated with traces (span-to-profile linking: "show me the CPU profile for this slow span").

What you get: "compare CPU by function for version 412 vs 411", "which function's share grew after Tuesday's deploy", and fleet-wide cost optimisation. Teams have reported meaningful compute savings from finding a few hot functions this way, but your numbers depend entirely on your code, so measure before and after.

## Trade-offs and when not to profile
- Profile **after** you know where the problem is coarsely (metrics and traces). Profiling a service that is slow because of a downstream dependency wastes time.
- Do not optimise from intuition; do not optimise from a profile of a debug build or an idle machine either. Reproduce realistic load.
- Heap snapshots **pause the process** and can be several times the heap size; take them on an instance removed from the load balancer.
- Profiling endpoints (`/debug/pprof`, `--inspect`) are dangerous if exposed publicly: bind to localhost or an internal port.

## Common mistakes
- Reading the flame graph x-axis as time.
- Looking at total time instead of self time and "optimising" a function that is just a caller.
- Missing off-CPU time: the request is slow because it waits on a lock or a pool, and the CPU profile looks clean.
- Taking one heap snapshot and calling the biggest object a leak; you need growth over time.
- Restarting pods on OOM forever instead of fixing the leak.
- Micro-optimising code that accounts for 2% of samples.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** a systematic approach (metrics and traces first, then profile), the ability to read a flame graph correctly, and a concrete method for memory leaks.

**60-second answer outline:**
1. Confirm the symptom with metrics: CPU, event loop lag, heap, GC; use traces to find the slow service and span.
2. CPU profile under realistic load (sampling profiler, flame graph): wide top frames are hot self time; x-axis is not time.
3. If CPU is low but latency high, look off-CPU: locks, pools, I/O.
4. For leaks, three heap snapshots, compare retained objects, follow retainers; common culprits are unbounded maps, listeners, timers, closures.
5. Continuous profiling in production to compare versions and catch regressions.

**Follow-ups to expect:** How do you read a flame graph? How would you find a memory leak in a Node.js service that gets OOM-killed every six hours? What is the difference between a flame graph and a flame chart? What overhead does continuous profiling add?

deepDives.title: Metrics before sampling: why the spanmetrics connector sits in front of tail sampling
deepDives.body:
Tail sampling deliberately keeps a biased sample: every error, every slow trace, and a small fraction of the rest. If you compute request rate and error ratio from the *stored* traces, errors look many times more common than they are and latency percentiles are skewed upwards.

```text
100,000 requests: 500 errors (0.5%), 1,000 slow
kept after tail sampling: 500 errors + 1,000 slow + 5% of 98,500 = ~6,425 traces
error ratio computed from kept traces: 500 / 6,425 = 7.8%   <-- wrong by ~15x
```

So the Collector pipeline forks: all spans flow into the `spanmetrics` connector, which emits exact RED histograms and counters to Prometheus, and *then* the traces pipeline applies tail sampling before export to Tempo. Exemplars on those histograms point at trace ids that were kept. The alternative, exporting metrics directly from the SDK (prom-client or OTel metrics), is also exact; the important rule is that no count you alert on is derived from sampled data without re-weighting.

Trade-off: spanmetrics labels come from span attributes, so the same cardinality discipline applies. Configure dimensions explicitly (`http.route`, `http.response.status_code` class, `service.name`) and never let `user.id` leak into them.

deepDives.title: Propagating context through the queue
deepDives.body:
HTTP auto-instrumentation propagates `traceparent` for free; message queues often do not, or do it in a way your consumer ignores. Without it the worker produces orphan traces and you lose the causal link between "order placed" and "email failed".

The fix is explicit: on publish, create a PRODUCER span and inject the active context into message headers with `propagation.inject(context.active(), headers)`; on consume, extract it with `propagation.extract(ROOT_CONTEXT, headers)` and start a CONSUMER span. Then choose **parent vs link**: for one-message-one-job processing, making the producer span the parent gives a single readable tree. For batch consumers that process 100 messages in one span, use **span links** to each producer context, because a span can only have one parent.

Two failure modes to test: retries (each delivery attempt should be its own consumer span with an attempt attribute) and dead-letter queues (keep the original headers so the DLQ replay joins the original trace). Long delays between produce and consume make traces span minutes or hours; backends handle this, but trace-level tail sampling cannot wait that long, so the worker's sampling decision follows the propagated sampled flag.

deepDives.title: Choosing SLOs and alert thresholds without paging yourself to death
deepDives.body:
Start from the user journey, not the service: "place an order" is the SLI, measured at the gateway as non-5xx responses under 800 ms over valid requests. Pick the initial SLO from history: if the last four weeks were 99.95% good, a 99.9% SLO leaves headroom; a 99.99% target would put you permanently in budget deficit.

With 99.9% over 30 days, the budget is 0.1% of requests. A 14.4x burn over 1 hour consumes 2% of the month's budget, a 6x burn over 6 hours consumes 5%, and a 1x burn over 3 days consumes 10%. The first two page, the third opens a ticket. Each alert requires both its long and short window (1/12 of the long one) to exceed the threshold, so a fixed problem stops paging within minutes.

In a demo the traffic is low, which makes ratios jumpy: one failure in 50 requests is a 2% error ratio and a 20x burn. Guard alerts with a minimum request rate (`and sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) > 1`) and drive steady background traffic with k6 so the drills behave like production. Finally, measure the alerts themselves: count pages per drill and false positives, and write that number in the README.

deepDives.title: Cardinality budget and cost report
deepDives.body:
Telemetry cost scales with active series, log bytes and stored spans, so the project tracks all three on a "cost" dashboard.

```text
metric series   = sum over metrics of product(label values) x (buckets + 2 for histograms)
example         = http duration: 25 routes x 4 status classes x 3 methods x 12 = 3,600 series per service
```

Guard rails: `prometheus_tsdb_head_series` graphed with an alert at a set budget, `sample_limit` on each scrape job so a bad deploy cannot add a million series, and `metric_relabel_configs` to drop labels you did not approve. In the Collector, a transform or attributes processor rewrites raw URLs to route templates before spanmetrics sees them.

For logs: drop health checks and static asset requests, keep 100% of WARN and ERROR, and sample successful canonical lines at 10% with a `sample_rate` field. Record before and after numbers for each optimisation; those numbers become your resume bullets.
